title: The Periodic Table
strapline: Why the table is arranged as it is, and how that arrangement lets you predict.
bigIdea: The Periodic Table is not a list — it is a prediction machine. Position tells you about properties, and properties repeat in patterns.
futureLearning: GCSE: electronic structure explains group number and reactivity trends; ionic bonding of Group 1 and 7.

misconceptions.misconception: The Periodic Table is ordered by when elements were discovered, or alphabetically.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils see no visible logic in the layout.
misconceptions.addressIt: Run the Mendeleev card-sorting activity so pupils rediscover the ordering principle themselves.

misconceptions.misconception: All metals are hard, shiny and magnetic.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Iron is the archetype for 'metal' in everyday life.
misconceptions.addressIt: Show sodium (soft, cut with a knife) and mercury footage; test a range of metals for magnetism and find most are not magnetic.

misconceptions.misconception: Group 1 metals get less reactive down the group, like the halogens.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils learn one trend and over-apply it.
misconceptions.addressIt: Tabulate the two trends side by side and require the direction to be stated with the group every time.

misconceptions.misconception: The transition metals are a group with shared reactivity like Group 1.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: They are a block, so pupils treat them as one group.
misconceptions.addressIt: Contrast: Group 1 reactivity trend is predictable; transition metals are characterised by shared property types (coloured compounds, catalysts), not a trend.

keyVocabulary.definition: A vertical column in the Periodic Table; elements in a group have similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row in the Periodic Table.
An element in Group 1; reacts with water to form an alkaline solution and hydrogen.
An element in Group 7; a reactive non-metal that forms salts with metals.
An element in Group 0; very unreactive.
A pattern in a property as you move down a group or across a period.

practicals.title: Group 1 metals with water
apparatus: large trough or safety screen tank
hazards: Alkali metals react violently; hydrogen ignites
control: Teacher demonstration only, behind safety screens, pupils 2 m back and seated
Use pieces no larger than a grain of rice
Keep the stock bottle closed and away from the trough; never use rubidium or caesium in school

practicals.title: Testing metals and non-metals
apparatus: samples of copper, magnesium, iron, carbon, sulfur, iodine (sealed)
control: Goggles; iodine viewed in a sealed tube only
Use a cloth over samples when hammering

practicals.title: The pH of metal and non-metal oxides
apparatus: sulfur (burned in a gas jar) or prepared sulfurous solution
hazards: Sulfur dioxide is an irritant — prepare in a fume cupboard
control: Teacher prepares the non-metal oxide solutions in advance in a fume cupboard

formative: Predict-then-check tasks before each Group 1 demonstration.
Trend sentence drill: 'As you go down Group 1, reactivity ... because ...'
Blank Periodic Table labelling against the clock.

summative.title: Periodic Table assessment
summative.style: 25 marks, 35 minutes, including one prediction question about an unfamiliar element.
summative.markSchemeNotes: Credit predictions that are justified by position even where the recalled fact is imperfect.

lessons.title: Mendeleev's puzzle
objectives: Explain the principles Mendeleev used to arrange the elements
Explain why leaving gaps was a scientific strength

sequence.detail: Symbol recall against the clock.
Card sort of element property cards with names hidden; pupils devise their own arrangement and justify it.
Reveal Mendeleev's ordering by atomic mass with gaps; his prediction of eka-silicon and its later confirmation.
Discussion: why was predicting an undiscovered element more impressive than just sorting the known ones?

keyQuestions: What did Mendeleev do that earlier chemists did not?
Why was leaving a gap braver than filling it?
support: Cards pre-sorted into two of the required columns.
challenge: Identify the pairs Mendeleev placed out of strict mass order and suggest why.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph on how Mendeleev's prediction was tested.
lessons.exitTicket: State the property Mendeleev ordered his elements by.

lessons.title: Groups, periods, metals and non-metals
objectives: Locate groups and periods on the Periodic Table
Describe the position of metals and non-metals
retrieval: What did Mendeleev order elements by?

sequence.detail: Three questions on Mendeleev plus two symbol recalls.
Structure of the table; the staircase dividing metals from non-metals; Groups 1, 7 and 0 named.
Colour-code and label a blank Periodic Table; locate ten given elements by group and period.
Rapid location quiz: 'Which element is in Group 2, Period 3?'

keyQuestions: Are there more metals or non-metals?
Where would you look for an unreactive gas?
support: Table with the staircase already drawn.
challenge: Research why hydrogen is placed awkwardly and argue where it should go.
lessons.homework: Complete and learn the labelled Periodic Table.
lessons.exitTicket: Name the element in Group 1, Period 2.

lessons.title: Properties of metals and non-metals
objectives: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals
Use evidence to classify an unknown element
retrieval: Where are non-metals found on the table?

sequence.detail: Location quiz on the table.
Test six samples for appearance, conductivity, malleability and state; record in a results table designed by pupils.
Identify the pattern; classify a seventh 'unknown' sample from its results.
Exit ticket.

keyQuestions: Which property is the most reliable test for a metal?
Which sample did not fit the pattern, and why might that be?
challenge: Research a metalloid and explain why it resists classification.
lessons.homework: Comparison table of five properties for metals and non-metals.
lessons.exitTicket: Give two properties that distinguish a metal from a non-metal.

lessons.title: Group 1: the alkali metals
objectives: Describe the reactions of Group 1 metals with water
Describe and explain the trend in reactivity down Group 1
Predict the behaviour of an unobserved member of the group

sequence.detail: Four questions on metals and table structure.
Pupils predict and commit in writing before seeing anything: which of Li, Na, K reacts most vigorously?
Lithium, sodium and potassium with water behind screens; universal indicator added; observations recorded in a common table.
Word equations for all three; the trend stated formally; introduce the alkaline product.
Predict the behaviour of rubidium, with justification from the trend.

keyQuestions: What gas is produced, and how would you test for it?
Why is the solution alkaline afterwards?
Why is caesium never demonstrated in schools?
support: Observation table with prompts for fizzing, movement, flame and indicator colour.
challenge: Write balanced symbol equations for all three reactions.
lessons.homework: Write word equations for lithium, sodium and potassium with water and with oxygen.
lessons.exitTicket: Complete: 'As you go down Group 1, reactivity ...'

lessons.title: Group 7 and Group 0
objectives: Describe the trend in reactivity down Group 7
Explain why Group 0 elements are unreactive and where they are used
retrieval: Name the gas produced when sodium reacts with water.

sequence.detail: Group 1 trend and equations recalled in writing.
Halogen appearance and state down the group; the reactivity trend, deliberately contrasted with Group 1. Noble gases and their uses.
Data table of halogen properties: describe two trends and use them to predict astatine's appearance and state.
Compare-and-contrast grid: Group 1 vs Group 7 vs Group 0 on reactivity, state and type of element.

keyQuestions: Why do Group 1 and Group 7 trends run in opposite directions?
Why is helium used in balloons rather than hydrogen?
support: Trend sentence stems supplied for both groups.
challenge: Predict the products of a displacement reaction between chlorine and potassium bromide and justify.
lessons.homework: Summary table of the three groups covered.
lessons.exitTicket: Which is more reactive, fluorine or iodine? Explain using the trend.

lessons.title: Metal and non-metal oxides
objectives: Describe the acidity of metal and non-metal oxides
Relate oxide behaviour to position in the Periodic Table

sequence.detail: Five questions spanning Lessons 2 to 5.
Add universal indicator to solutions of metal oxides and prepared non-metal oxide solutions; record pH.
Metal oxides tend to be basic or alkaline; non-metal oxides tend to be acidic. Link to acid rain as a real-world consequence.
Predict the pH of the oxide of an unseen element given only its position.

keyQuestions: Predict the pH of sodium oxide solution; justify from position.
Why does burning fossil fuel containing sulfur cause acid rain?
support: pH colour chart at each bench; results table supplied.
challenge: Research amphoteric oxides and explain why aluminium oxide breaks the rule.
lessons.homework: Explain how the Periodic Table lets you predict whether an oxide will be acidic.
lessons.exitTicket: Metal oxides are usually ... and non-metal oxides are usually ...

lessons.title: Review and assessment
objectives: Consolidate knowledge of the Periodic Table
Apply trends to predict properties of unfamiliar elements

sequence.detail: Blank Periodic Table labelling plus trend sentences from memory.
25-mark assessment.
Immediate whole-class feedback on the prediction question.

support: Periodic table permitted for all pupils in the assessment.
challenge: Design a Periodic Table for a fictional set of elements from property data.
lessons.exitTicket: Which trend do you still need to practise?
